title: Challenge: Gray Code

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only gray-code program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Consecutive generated codes differ in exactly one bit. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `n=2`, the worked program returns `0,1,3,2`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `n=3`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Parse n and return n-bit binary-reflected Gray code order. For n=0 return the single code 0.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Parse n and return n-bit binary-reflected Gray code order. For n=0 return the single code 0. On input `n=3`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Map i to i xor (i shifted right) so neighboring codes differ by one bit. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. An arithmetic or bitwise transformation relies on an identity. Write that identity and the domain in which it holds. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(2^n) time · O(2^n) output; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Test zero, one, powers of two, maximum input size, and overflow or underflow around intermediate products. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `0,1,3,2,6,7,5,4,12,13,15,14,10,11,9,8`. Consecutive generated codes differ in exactly one bit. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: For three bits, i=0..7 maps to 0,1,3,2,6,7,5,4. Each adjacent pair differs by one bit, including the last-to-first transition for positive bit width. Zero bits yields the single code 0.
